technical.clientSecretHandling: Web application clients must send the client secret at the token endpoint. Google shows the secret only once at creation, so store it in a secret manager immediately. PKCE is documented for installed apps (S256 or plain).

refreshTokens.expiry: 7 days after consent while an External app is in Testing; otherwise until revoked, unused for six months, the user changes password (Gmail scopes), or a token limit is exceeded
refreshTokens.notes: Only returned with access_type=offline and only on the first code exchange; use prompt=consent to get a new one. Limit of 100 per Google Account per client ID; the oldest is silently invalidated.

technical.accessTokenLifetime: Read expires_in from the token response (about 1 hour); no fixed lifetime
redirectUriRules: Must exactly match an Authorized redirect URI, including scheme, case and trailing slash
No raw IP hosts (except localhost IPs), wildcards, fragments, userinfo or path traversal
Hosts can't be under googleusercontent.com and TLDs must be on the public suffix list

profiles.intent: Read users' mail (gmail.readonly, restricted scope) for any Google user

scopes.name: https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.readonly
scopes.purpose: Read messages, threads and settings; also accepted by users.getProfile for the Stage 1 check. Classified Restricted.

testModeLimits.text: Testing status: only listed test users (up to 100) can authorize, they see an unverified-app warning, and refresh tokens expire 7 days after consent.

configGotchas.text: Add access_type=offline (and prompt=consent if you've authorized before) or you get no refresh token.
Copy the client secret at creation; it can't be viewed again.
Refresh tokens issued in Testing die after 7 days; this is expected, not a bug.

stage1.summary: Self-serve: create a project, enable the Gmail API, configure branding in Testing with yourself as a test user, create a Web client and complete one code flow. Restricted scopes work in Testing without verification.

stage2.summary: Going public with gmail.readonly needs brand verification, restricted scope review, and an annual CASA security assessment from a third-party lab that you pay. Until then you're capped at 100 users for the project's lifetime.

time.range: Several weeks; the security assessment alone takes 2-8 weeks
time.startsWhen: after you submit the data access request in the Verification Center; the assessment starts only when Google Trust and Safety contacts you

stage1DoneWhen.text: GET https://gmail.googleapis.com/gmail/v1/users/me/profile with your access token returns 200 with your emailAddress and messagesTotal, and your token response included a refresh_token.

blockedBy.how: Google reviews the use case and scope justification and can reject it, assigns the CASA level, and caps unverified apps at 100 users for the project's lifetime.
Workspace admins can block your app, limit it to unrestricted services, or restrict Gmail so only trusted apps can reach it, which revokes existing tokens.
You must own and verify the domain, publish a compliant privacy policy, record the demo video, follow Limited Use, and pay a CASA lab every year.

profiles.bottomLine: A first token takes one sitting in Testing mode. Going public with gmail.readonly means restricted scope review plus a third-party CASA assessment you pay for every year, and several weeks of lead time.
topRisks: Unverified apps can only ever onboard 100 users, and that cap can't be reset
The annual CASA assessment is a recurring cost, about $540 to $40k
Workspace admins can block the app or restrict Gmail for their whole organization

steps.title: Create a Cloud project and enable the Gmail API
instructions: Sign in to the Google Cloud console and create (or pick) a project for this app.
Go to APIs & Services > Library > Google Workspace, click Gmail API, then Enable. Or run gcloud services enable gmail.googleapis.com.

steps.title: Set up Google Auth platform branding
instructions: Open Menu > Google Auth platform > Branding. If you see Get Started, click it.
Enter the App name and User support email, click Next.
Under Audience choose External (any Google user), click Next.
Under Contact Information enter an email for project notices, click Next.
Check I agree to the Google API Services: User Data Policy, click Continue, then Create.

steps.title: Add yourself as a test user
instructions: Go to Audience. Leave Publishing status as Testing.
Under Test users click Add users, enter your Google account email, then Save.
Only listed test users (up to 100) can authorize while in Testing, and their refresh tokens expire after 7 days.

steps.title: Declare gmail.readonly under Data Access
instructions: Go to Data Access and click Add or Remove Scopes.
Add https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.readonly and click Save. It will be listed as a restricted scope.
Don't add scopes you won't use now; every scope must be justified at verification.

steps.title: Create a Web application OAuth client
instructions: Go to Google Auth platform > Clients and click Create Client.
Set Application type to Web application and enter a Name (only shown in the console).
Under Authorized redirect URIs add your callback exactly as your app sends it: HTTPS (http only for localhost), no wildcards, fragments or raw IPs; trailing slash and case must match.
Leave Use this client for an AI-powered agent unchecked unless it applies; it can't be changed later.
Click Create and copy the client ID and client secret now. The secret is shown only once; keep it in a secret manager, never in source control.

steps.title: Send yourself through the consent flow
instructions: Open https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth?client_id=CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=YOUR_URI&response_type=code&scope=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.readonly&access_type=offline&prompt=consent&state=RANDOM (URL-encode values).
access_type=offline is needed for a refresh token; prompt=consent makes Google prompt again so a new code can return one if you've authorized before.
Optionally add PKCE (code_challenge with code_challenge_method=S256). Web clients still send the client secret.
Sign in as your test user. Expect an unverified-app warning; continue past it. Check that state on the redirect matches.

steps.title: Exchange the code for tokens
instructions: POST to https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token with client_id, client_secret, code, the same redirect_uri and grant_type=authorization_code (plus code_verifier if you used PKCE).
Store access_token, expires_in and refresh_token server-side. Refresh with grant_type=refresh_token before expires_in runs out.
In Testing, the refresh token dies 7 days after consent; plan to re-consent during development.

steps.title: Check the token reads the mailbox
instructions: GET https://gmail.googleapis.com/gmail/v1/users/me/profile with Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN.
Expect 200 with emailAddress, messagesTotal, threadsTotal and historyId.

steps.title: Prepare homepage, privacy policy and domain verification
instructions: Host a public homepage on a domain you own that describes the app (not just a login page).
Publish a privacy policy on the same domain, linked from the homepage, disclosing how you access, use, store and share Gmail data and that you follow Limited Use.
Verify each authorized domain in Google Search Console as a project owner or editor.
Add the homepage, privacy policy and authorized domains on the Branding page.

steps.title: Verify and publish branding
instructions: On the Branding page click Verify Branding. Automated checks usually finish in minutes; manual review usually takes 2-3 business days.
If it shows Need to fix issues, click View issues, fix, and re-verify (or request additional review).
Click Publish branding within 7 days of a compliant result, or it reverts to Need to re-verify.

steps.title: Move the app to In production
instructions: On Audience, click Publish app to switch Publishing status from Testing to In production.
Until restricted scope verification completes, users see the unverified-app screen and only 100 new users can ever authorize.

steps.title: Submit the data access (restricted scope) request
instructions: In the Verification Center, open data access status and start the request (needs published branding).
Declare every scope, select your application type, and explain why gmail.metadata or other narrower scopes won't work. Don't request scopes for unbuilt features.
Upload an unlisted YouTube demo video in English showing the app name, client ID in the address bar, the full consent screen with gmail.readonly, and the feature that uses it.
Answer follow-up emails from the review team promptly.

steps.title: Pass the CASA security assessment
instructions: Wait for Google Trust and Safety to tell you to start; it's the last step, and Google sets your assurance level (AL1 or AL2).
Engage a CASA authorized lab (e.g. Bishop Fox, DEKRA, NetSentries, TAC Security) and pay its fee, about $540 to $40k.
Fix findings, get the Letter of Validation, and submit it to Google Trust and Safety.
Existing SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001 or HITRUST reports can shorten the work.

steps.title: Recertify every 12 months
instructions: Google emails when recertification is due, 12 months from your last Letter of Validation's effective date.
The reassessment is a full test regardless of changes, and you pay the lab again. Keep Owner and Editor contacts current.

nuances.text: The console menu is now Google Auth platform (Branding, Audience, Data Access, Clients, Verification Center). "OAuth consent screen" in older text means these pages.
Every Gmail scope that reads mail content or headers outside add-ons is restricted, including gmail.metadata, so there's no lighter-review path for reading mail.
The security assessment is tied to storing or transmitting restricted data on servers. A server-side integration does both, so plan on it.
Google returns a refresh token only on the first code exchange. If you lose it, the user must consent again; prompt=consent forces a new consent screen.
The 100 refresh tokens per account per client limit silently invalidates the oldest, so don't mint a fresh token per session or per worker.
PKCE is optional for web clients; they still need the client secret.
The assessment result is called a Letter of Validation or Letter of Assessment; tiers appear as AL1/AL2 or tier-2/tier-3. Same thing.
Assessment cost varies by lab: about $540/year at the low end, $8k-$40k from other labs.
Tier 2 self-scanning ended in May 2024; expect to hire a lab.

No verification is needed for internal apps (Internal user type), personal use by a few people you know, or testing. Domain-wide installation skips brand verification but not restricted scope verification.
Adding redirect URIs, renaming the app, or changing scopes after verification can trigger re-verification; a new restricted scope can trigger reassessment.
Clients have a one-way Use this client for an AI-powered agent setting at creation.
